comment_summary: Group pages produced stuttering audio, and investigation traced the problem to the Windows version of FreeSWITCH, which cannot launch or schedule the separate processing threads needed to record the caller (A-Leg) while the paged devices (B-Legs) stream simultaneously; the same configuration ran perfectly every time on Linux. A long configuration-only search for a workaround proved non-viable, so a revised paging model was prototyped in which FreeSWITCH records the page to .wav files and VoIP Service acts as the control point, opening and closing B-Leg channels, timing the page, and cleaning up the streaming files. Testing confirmed the new model pages without stutter at the cost of a 1-2 second delay before audio opens and some wander between devices because each streams independently, and a small dialplan change allows flipping back to the original model for comparison. The thread notes no OS tweak or configuration setting can prioritize the audio and that the stutter could occur with as few as two devices, and the issue was ultimately closed as resolved by the 4.2.000 upgrade.

Investigation reproduced it only after setting a new VoIP extension range and then creating paging groups before saving devices, so the devices had no VoIP addresses yet; one view was that this is expected behavior and the user must save devices first. Reviewers argued the scenario is easy for a customer to hit and could result in pages going to every room, and asked for a clearer ECT warning message. impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
Multi-room paging in Nurse Call was using a conference bridge to establish an audio page using FreeSWITCH.  It is a simple model and requires minimum setup effort. Unfortunately, FreeSWITCH in Windows has an issue related to audio pacing of conference calls.  At the OS level, Windows cannot reliably feed the audio stream to the devices.  A buffer underrun occurs which causes momentary gaps that sound like a stutter.  The issue is deeper than task priority, RAM, or CPU core affinity of which no adjustments can fix the issue reliably.

To address this problem, an alternate strategy is needed that avoids the pacing (at least until we can move to containers based on Linux which do not have the pacing problem).  The change involves separating the recording of the page from the participant playback. The following describes how it works.  
1\. When the page is initiated, audio from the caller is recorded to .wav files local to FreeSWITCH.  The .wav files contain one second of the audio from the caller.  
2\. After 1 second of audio has been recorded, the participating devices are invited to start playing the audio stream.  As soon as each device joins, it plays back the audio files starting from the beginning.  
3\. When the caller completes his/her page and hangs up, the audio files stop being recorded.  
4\. Participating devices continue to play back the audio files until all of the audio is played out and then they hang up.  
5\. As soon as all of the participating devices have closed audio and detected as hung-up, the collection of paging audio files is removed.

Due to latency in processing the invite and the fact that a device plays the whole page regardless of when they begin, there can be an odd delay in the audio playback.  This is different than the previous model in which delayed participants would not receive the first part of the page if they joined late. 

If the VoIP Service is shutdown or crashes while in the middle of a page, it loses knowledge/understanding of the existence of the page.  This does not affect the end-of-page processing for the devices.  They will close as soon as they reach the end of the audio files.  However, special consideration is needed regarding the audio files that were produced.  When VoIP Service starts/re-starts, it checks to see if there are any existing audio page files.  If there are any, it will remove them as part of service initialization.

comment_summary: A site reported a 4-5 second delay in paging audio. Wireshark analysis measured an average delay of about 3 seconds and established this as expected behavior, because a fix for stuttering paging audio introduced a deliberate 2 seconds of silence transmitted before audio is sent at the start of a page, plus roughly another second for the full audio path to be established after invites go out. The investigator confirmed the captured performance meets expected performance levels and that no further investigation is required. The thread notes 3CX was definitely faster than the current FreeSWITCH solution at opening a page, that the 1-2 second delay figure is informal and not documented in release notes, and that the stated long-term fix is to move FreeSWITCH to Linux.

summary: Authentication Failure on push config causes multiple thread of execution.
description: This appears to have been caused by a change made by SecureBlackBox in the updated version we are now using is triggering the delivery of two contradictory events. The gist of it is, when the authentication failure described above occurs, a callback that wasn't getting called in a previous version is now getting called. Our code in that callback, on an authentication failure, is to fire off a completion event with an error state of 'Authentication Failure.' What is happening at the same time is that the main-line code is continuing to process and it checks to see if all download attempts (3) have been tried before giving up. So, it fires off another Download attempt. The authentication failure completion event cleans up resources needed by the Download event and, boom, we have a problem.



Based on assessment to date, we expect to see a lost device system alert (due to device registration failures) prior to the config push. Appears to be a precursor with the exception of a checksum error on the configuration file that’s pushed to the device.
comment_summary: The defect is that an authentication failure during a push of configuration causes multiple threads of execution. Commentary stressed the scope and field impact: the problem can occur on any ECT config push, including MAC and break-fix service activity rather than just planned upgrades, and devices in recovery mode cannot always be identified or replaced beforehand because the parts and labor are billable without a GOLD level SMA. It was also noted that upgrading to 4.1.200 changes the extension format from 3CX to FreeSwitch, so any device that fails to receive its config is left with no audio, which was argued to carry a potential safety impact. The defect was tested and verified in nc_pd_release_4.1.210_5/ST3 and closed as Done.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
The authentication service currently calls ValidateCredentials (username, password) to check LDAP credentials.  
There is a third parameter, ContextOptions, which we do not use.  
This parameter controls what protocol the ValidateCredentials call uses.  
See [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices.accountmanagement.contextoptions?view=net-9.0-pp](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices.accountmanagement.contextoptions?view=net-9.0-pp).  
The fixed code will try the ValidateCredentials (username, password) call, but if that call throws an exception,  
it will be caught, and the other form of ValidateCredentials (username, password, ContextOptions) will be tried.  
ContextOptions is an enum that can be parsed from a string, and this value will be in the Settings.xml file  
for the AuthenticationService as key 'RetryContextOptions' with a default value of 1  (which is negotiate, which will go over NTLM or Kerberos, not SSL).

comment_summary: A site converted from NCM to VNC experienced widespread short-lived RCB Switch Disconnect alerts and random RCB3/GRS7 reboots, which the customer called phantom calls. A long investigation ruled out wiring, recrimping, additional and replacement PoE switches, cable type (found to be CAT6 Superslim), the firewall and the smoke alarm interface, while swapping a trouble room from RCB3/GRS7 to RCB2/GRS5 made the problem disappear and the reverse swap made a quiet room start alarming. Evidence collected included GRS7 brownout events, ntpdate step time adjustments of over 500 days at each restart, device reboots with no exception logs as if power had been lost, and a correlation with rooms configured with a supervised fire alarm push button switch. The issue was finally resolved by disabling all security scanning on the PoE switch and the downstream Linux-based nurse call devices (the Linux-side scanning had been missed earlier) and hard power cycling the PoE switch, after which the unit ran about 39 days without a random reboot.

rca_review_comments: A software design defect was identified in the Nurse Call system's handling of dome lights and zone lights on RCB2 hardware. Following a reboot or power cycle of a room containing both a dome light and a zone light, call-tone associations could become incorrectly initialized. As a result, Code Blue (and other configured) calls placed from a zoned room triggered audible tones on an unrelated dome light, even though the dome light did not illuminate and the zone light functioned as configured. The condition persisted until a call was placed from the rebooted room, which restored the correct call-tone mapping. The issue was reproducible across multiple floors at Stanford 500P Hospital and was documented under defect **CWS-BUG-2109**

When logging is turned up to everything in verbose mode the rcb3 can experience a seg fault.  Turning up logging this high is not recommended because of how much it can affect performance.  But the log should be fixed if this is needed for short periods for debugging.

root_cause_summary: Bad U1_PWR and bad audio amplifier U9_AUD likely due to an ESD event or hot plugging or a known issue with the bed connector cable (bent pins).
investigation_details: **HW Investigation**

Device would not power up because all power rails were shorted to Ground, which trips fuse RT1. So it failed to initialize on the DFCT (no logs to attach). Confirmed with DMM continuity test that U1_PWR input and output were shorted (pins 2 and 4). Removed U1_PWR and +5V rail was still shorted to Ground but other power rails were normal resistance. U9_AUD was removed and +5V rail and ground were no longer shorted.

Replaced U1_PWR and U9_AUD with known good components. Device now passes DFCT tests, see attached logs. Note that VPD read/write test was skipped in case there were other issues that required firmware investigation.

We have seen this issue before, resulting from bent pins on the bed connector cable, hot plugging, ESD, etc. (Reference https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1866, https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1685, https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1075  and others.)

Conclusion: Bad U1_PWR and bad audio amplifier U9_AUD likely due to an ESD event or hot plugging or a known issue with the bed connector cable (bent pins).

**Steps taken by Oliver T.**  
Fairbanks is installing a new campus on an existing server running NNC 3.9.401 with NaviCare devices (RCB3s, SRSs, and GRS10s).   
Some of the semi-private rooms have dual SRSs off of the RCB3. In locations with dual SRSs, one of the SRSs has noticeably lower audio volume/quality than the other.  
This happens for SRSs on both RS1 and RS2 depending on the room, we're not sure why the issue presents on different RS ports in different rooms.

I thought it might be a power issue at first. This was supported by the fact that we were seeing brown outs and SRSs not booting.   
We troubleshot and eventually replaced the customer's unsupported Cisco 9300-48P (PoE+) switches with supported Cisco 9300-48U (UPoE) switches.   
We confirmed that the brown outs were resolved and that the RCB3s are now negotiating four pair power, however, the audio issue remains.

Here are some of the other things we've tried:

Reboot RCB3 (no good)  
Re-push firmware (no good)  
Replace RCB3 (no good)  
Move RCB3 and SRS to Hillrom switches (maybe good, inconsistent feedback from onsite resource)  
Test GRS10s on Cisco and Hillrom switches (no good)  
Test with different GRS10s (no good)  
Confirmed NTP (date and time correct, customer does not use low volume period)  
Increased unit volume from 70 to 90 (did increase volume but some SRSs are still noticeably different)  
Captured audio from the VoIP server (audio sounds consistent in the captures)  
Unplugged working SRS and tested rooms with only the non-working SRS (no good, non working SRS still doesn't work)  
This is another indication that it might not be power related

It seems that the issue only occurs when connected to Ciscos, but there has been inconsistent feedback on testing and I'm not confident in saying the switch is the problem.   
That being said, we haven't looked at QoS or packet manipulation yet so that's TBD.
